lessonTitle: The Acute Scrotum and Urinary Retention

blocks.text: A 14-year-old arrives at 11 a.m. with pain that began at 3 a.m. He was too embarrassed to wake his parents. His left testis is swollen, hard and sits high. Every hour of that silence mattered, because a twisted testis is a blood-starved testis.

blocks.markdown:
**Two emergencies, one theme: time.** The *acute scrotum* is any sudden painful scrotal swelling, and the commonest dangerous cause is *testicular torsion*. *Acute urinary retention* is the sudden inability to pass urine. Both are diagnosed largely at the bedside, both are treated by a simple procedure, and in both a delay converts a reversible problem into permanent damage.

The testis hangs on the **spermatic cord**, which carries the testicular artery, the pampiniform venous plexus, the vas deferens and nerves. It is normally anchored to the posterior scrotal wall because the tunica vaginalis attaches only to its posterior surface.

blocks.title: Testicular torsion
blocks.text: Twisting of the spermatic cord, which cuts off the testicular blood supply. The usual predisposition is the *bell-clapper deformity*: the tunica vaginalis surrounds the whole testis and lower cord, so the testis is not fixed posteriorly and can rotate freely inside the sac. The deformity is often bilateral, which is why the other side is fixed too.

blocks.markdown:
**Mechanism, then clinical picture.** Rotation first occludes the low-pressure veins, so the testis swells; then arterial inflow is lost and the tissue becomes ischaemic. Ischaemia causes sudden severe pain, often with nausea, vomiting and lower abdominal pain (shared visceral innervation), which can mislead the unwary into an abdominal work-up.

Typical findings: a tender, swollen, **high-riding testis with a horizontal lie**, an **absent cremasteric reflex** (stroking the inner thigh does not elevate the testis), and pain not relieved by lifting the testis. Torsion peaks in adolescence but occurs at any age, including neonates, and any male with acute scrotal pain is torsion until proven otherwise.

rows: Sudden, often at night or after exertion
Gradual over a day or more
Sexually active men; older men with urinary tract disease
Tender epididymis, then whole testis; erythema
Tender upper pole, sometimes a 'blue dot'
Antibiotics by sex and risk, analgesia (check current BASHH/BNF/local guidance)
blocks.caption: Differentiating the common causes of the acute scrotum

blocks.title: Worked example: a presentation within hours
blocks.prompt: A 16-year-old has had 5 hours of severe right scrotal pain with vomiting. The right testis is high and tender, the cremasteric reflex is absent on that side, and he is afebrile. Decide what happens next.

steps.text: Pattern recognition: sudden onset, vomiting, high horizontal lie and absent cremasteric reflex in an adolescent is torsion until proven otherwise.

Time matters: salvage is best in the first few hours and falls steeply with delay (often quoted as high within about 6 hours and low after about 24 hours; exact figures vary between series). Five hours has already elapsed, so every minute counts.

Do not delay for imaging: a Doppler ultrasound may be used if the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and it is available without delay, but it must never postpone theatre when the history and examination fit.

Act: keep him nil by mouth, give analgesia, obtain consent and call the urology/surgical team for immediate scrotal exploration. Manual detorsion may be attempted as a temporising step in some units, but exploration is still required.

At surgery: detort, assess viability (colour returns after warming), fix the testis (orchidopexy) and also fix the contralateral testis because of the bilateral anatomy; remove the testis (orchidectomy) only if it is clearly non-viable.

blocks.answer: Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy; imaging must not delay it.

blocks.markdown:
**Urinary retention.** Bladder emptying needs a contracting detrusor and an open outlet. Failure of either, or an inability to sense the bladder, causes retention. Common causes in men: benign prostatic enlargement, constipation, drugs (anticholinergics, opioids, some antihistamines and antidepressants), urinary tract infection, urethral stricture, clot, and neurological disease. In women, consider pelvic masses, prolapse, and post-operative or neurological causes.

The key distinction is between the **acute** and **chronic** forms.

blocks.title: Acute versus chronic retention
blocks.text: **Acute retention** is sudden, *painful* inability to pass urine with a palpable, tender bladder. **Chronic retention** develops slowly and is typically *painless*: the bladder holds a persistently large residual volume after voiding, often with poor stream, overflow incontinence or nocturnal enuresis. A residual volume of about 300 mL or more is often used as a working threshold, but cut-offs vary between guidelines. In *high-pressure* chronic retention the sustained bladder pressure transmits back and causes bilateral hydronephrosis and renal impairment.

rows: Poor stream, hesitancy, dribbling, overflow incontinence
Often several hundred mL, tends to be smaller than in chronic
Often large, sometimes over a litre
May show hydronephrosis and raised creatinine
Catheterise if symptomatic, renal impairment or very high residual; monitor for post-obstructive diuresis

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a drained volume
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old man with painless dribbling has a palpable bladder and creatinine above his baseline. A urethral catheter drains 1,500 mL in the first 2 hours; over the next 6 hours he passes a further 2,400 mL. Interpret.

steps.text: Painless, palpable bladder, overflow dribbling and a large volume point to chronic retention; the raised creatinine suggests high-pressure retention with obstructive uropathy.
Volumes: 1,500 mL in 2 h is 750 mL/h; 2,400 mL over 6 h is 400 mL/h. The urine output after relief is far above normal.
Interpretation: this is post-obstructive diuresis, from retained solute and fluid, osmotic load of urea and temporarily reduced tubular concentrating ability.

Management: strict fluid balance, regular weight and electrolytes (urea, creatinine, sodium, potassium), and intravenous fluid replacement only as needed according to local protocol; admission is usual. Image the renal tract and treat the underlying cause (often prostatic).

blocks.answer: Chronic high-pressure retention complicated by post-obstructive diuresis, managed with catheter, monitoring and admission.

blocks.markdown:
**Catheterisation.** A urethral catheter is a hollow tube passed through the urethra with a balloon that anchors it in the bladder. Indications include retention, accurate fluid monitoring in the acutely unwell, and perioperative use; it should not be used for convenience. Check for contraindications first: after pelvic or perineal trauma, blood at the meatus, a high-riding or boggy prostate and perineal bruising suggest urethral injury, so *do not pass a urethral catheter*; call urology, who may use a suprapubic route.

Size is given in Charrière (Ch, also French): the number equals the outer **circumference in mm**, so the diameter in mm is approximately the Ch value divided by 3.

blocks.caption: External diameter from Charrière size; circumference = $\pi d$

items: Explain and obtain consent; clean hands, sterile gloves, aseptic non-touch technique, chaperone as per local policy.
Clean the meatus; instil sterile lubricant with local anaesthetic gel and allow time for effect.
Hold the penis upright, advance the catheter gently to the hilt (the bifurcation), and only inflate the balloon once urine drains, so it is not inflated in the urethra.
Connect to a closed drainage system, record volume and character of urine, and always replace the foreskin to prevent paraphimosis.
Document the reason, size, balloon volume, and a plan for removal or review.

blocks.title: Complications to anticipate
blocks.text: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (the commonest; risk rises with each day, so remove as early as possible), false passage and urethral trauma, later urethral stricture, paraphimosis if the foreskin is left retracted, haematuria, bladder spasm, blockage or encrustation, and inflation of the balloon in the urethra (severe pain and trauma). Large drained volumes can produce haematuria or post-obstructive diuresis. Suprapubic catheters carry bowel-injury risk and are placed by trained staff.

points: Suspected torsion is a surgical emergency: exploration should not wait for imaging when the picture fits, and the contralateral testis is also fixed.
Acute retention is painful and sudden; chronic retention is painless, with a large residual volume and risk of hydronephrosis and post-obstructive diuresis.
Urethral catheterisation needs asepsis, lubrication, full insertion before balloon inflation, foreskin replacement, and caution if urethral injury is suspected; size in Ch is circumference in mm.
Antibiotic choices and local protocols should be checked against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old is brought in after 3 hours of sudden severe right testicular pain that began while he was asleep, with two episodes of vomiting. The right testis lies higher than the left and the right cremasteric reflex is absent. Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent surgical exploration of the scrotum
Wait for a scrotal ultrasound report before deciding
Oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
Reassure and give simple analgesia

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent surgical exploration of the scrotum

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the picture is classic for torsion and time is critical.
distractorRationale.b: Imaging must not delay theatre when clinical suspicion is high.
distractorRationale.c: This treats epididymo-orchitis, which is a gradual-onset, febrile illness.
distractorRationale.d: Torsion would be missed and the testis lost.

questions.explanation: Sudden onset, vomiting, a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex in an adolescent make torsion the working diagnosis. Salvage falls as ischaemia time lengthens, so urgent exploration with detorsion and bilateral fixation is indicated, and imaging should not delay it.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old has had two days of gradually worsening left scrotal pain, a temperature of 38.2 C and dysuria. The testis lies normally, the cremasteric reflex is intact, and the tenderness is maximal over the epididymis. Which feature most strongly favours epididymo-orchitis over torsion?

options.text: Gradual onset with fever and urinary symptoms
Pain radiating to the lower abdomen
Scrotal swelling
Nausea

questions.correctOptionText: Gradual onset with fever and urinary symptoms

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this pattern is typical of infection.
distractorRationale.b: Seen in torsion as well, so it does not discriminate.
distractorRationale.d: Can occur in either condition and is not discriminating.

questions.explanation: Epididymo-orchitis usually develops over a day or more with fever, urinary symptoms and a tender epididymis, whereas torsion is sudden. Swelling, pain referral and nausea overlap, and no single sign is reliable, so the overall pattern together with the cremasteric reflex and testis position guides the decision.

questions.stem: When clinical suspicion of testicular torsion is high, surgical exploration should proceed even if a scrotal ultrasound is not yet available or is equivocal.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Torsion is a clinical diagnosis in a high-probability case, and the cost of a negative exploration is small compared with that of a lost testis. Imaging may help when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain, but it must not introduce delay.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has had nocturnal dribbling and a weak stream for months. He has no pain. Examination finds a palpable, non-tender bladder reaching the umbilicus; creatinine is raised and ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis. After a urethral catheter is placed, which is the most important monitoring need?

options.text: Fluid balance and electrolytes for post-obstructive diuresis
Immediate bladder irrigation to prevent clot retention
Clamping the catheter hourly to train the bladder
Withholding all fluids for 24 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Fluid balance and electrolytes for post-obstructive diuresis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: large volumes of urine can follow relief and cause fluid and electrolyte depletion.
distractorRationale.b: Not routine without haematuria and clots.
distractorRationale.c: Clamping is not indicated and risks infection and discomfort.
distractorRationale.d: This would worsen the risk of dehydration.

questions.explanation: This is painless chronic high-pressure retention with obstructive uropathy. Relief of the obstruction may cause a large diuresis, so fluid balance, weight and electrolytes (and renal function) are monitored, usually in hospital, while the cause is investigated.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man 12 hours after hernia repair, who received opioid analgesia, is unable to pass urine and is in distress with suprapubic pain. Which feature most clearly marks this as acute rather than chronic retention?

options.text: Sudden, painful inability to void with a tender bladder
Overflow dribbling over several months
Bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound
A very large residual volume that built up slowly

questions.correctOptionText: Sudden, painful inability to void with a tender bladder

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acute retention is painful and sudden.
distractorRationale.c: This is a feature of chronic high-pressure retention.

questions.explanation: Acute retention is painful with a palpable, tender bladder and a clear precipitant such as opioids, constipation or surgery. Chronic retention is insidious and painless, often with overflow and renal changes. Management of the acute case is urgent catheterisation with attention to the cause.

questions.stem: A urethral catheter is sized as 16 Ch, where the Charrière number is the outer circumference in mm. Taking the circumference as pi times the diameter, estimate the external diameter in mm.
questions.explanation: The circumference is 16 mm, so d = 16/pi which is about 5.09 mm. The rule of thumb Ch/3 gives 5.33 mm, and both fall within a sensible tolerance of the key.

questions.stem: A man with chronic retention drains 1,800 mL of urine over the first 6 hours after catheterisation. Calculate his mean urine output in mL per hour.
questions.explanation: Mean output = 1,800 mL divided by 6 h = 300 mL/h. Persistently high output after relief of obstruction suggests post-obstructive diuresis and needs fluid and electrolyte monitoring; the exact threshold used to define it varies between sources.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man falls astride a bar and later cannot void. There is blood at the external urethral meatus and bruising of the perineum. A junior colleague suggests passing a urethral catheter. What is the best response?

options.text: Do not pass a urethral catheter; involve urology for imaging or suprapubic drainage
Pass the largest catheter available to tamponade the bleeding
Pass a catheter with extra lubricant and inflate the balloon early
Give an alpha-blocker and wait at home

questions.correctOptionText: Do not pass a urethral catheter; involve urology for imaging or suprapubic drainage

distractorRationale.b: Blind passage may convert a partial tear into a complete one.
distractorRationale.c: Forced passage worsens injury and inflation in the urethra is dangerous.
distractorRationale.d: He needs urgent assessment, not an outpatient trial without voiding.

questions.explanation: Blood at the meatus and perineal bruising after straddle trauma indicate possible urethral injury. A blind urethral catheter may worsen the damage, so urology are involved and imaging or suprapubic drainage is considered.

questions.stem: Describe the steps of male urethral catheterisation and list four complications.
markingGuide: Consent, explanation, hand hygiene, sterile gloves and aseptic technique; check contraindications such as suspected urethral injury
Clean the meatus and instil lubricating anaesthetic gel; wait for effect
Hold the penis upright and advance to the hilt; inflate the balloon only after urine drains
Connect to closed drainage, record volume, replace foreskin
Complications (any four): CAUTI, false passage, stricture, paraphimosis, haematuria, blockage, balloon inflated in urethra, bladder spasm
questions.explanation: A good answer follows a safe sequence from consent to documentation and states why each step prevents harm, such as avoiding balloon inflation in the urethra and replacing the foreskin. Complications should include infection and urethral trauma, which are the commonest and most serious.

questions.stem: Explain why testicular torsion is time-critical and what the operation involves, including management of the opposite testis.
markingGuide: Cord twist occludes venous then arterial supply, causing ischaemia, infarction and loss of the testis
Salvage falls with duration of ischaemia; prompt exploration matters (exact timings vary)
Diagnosis clinical; imaging not to delay surgery when suspicion high
Operation: scrotal exploration, detorsion, check viability, orchidopexy, orchidectomy if non-viable
Bilateral anatomy (bell-clapper), so the contralateral testis is fixed too
questions.explanation: The answer should link mechanism to outcome: venous then arterial occlusion causes irreversible ischaemia over hours. Because the predisposing anatomy is usually bilateral, the contralateral testis is also fixed at the same operation.
